items.title: The Pack
items.content: A game uses one pack of 52 cards. The pack holds four suits, and each suit holds thirteen cards. The four suits carry equal weight, so a suit never makes one hand beat another. Take every joker out of the pack before the deal.

items.title: The Order of the Cards
items.content: Card values run upward from two through ten, then jack, queen, king, and ace. The ace also counts as the lowest card in the sequence five, four, three, two, ace.

items.title: Hole Cards
items.content: The dealer gives each player two cards face down. These two cards are that player's hole cards. They belong to that player alone, and the player keeps them face down until the showdown.

items.title: The Order of the Deal
items.content: The dealer gives out the hole cards one at a time and moves clockwise. The first card goes to the player on the immediate left of the button.

items.title: The Board
items.content: Across one hand the dealer puts five cards face up in the middle of the table. These five cards are the board, and every player at the table shares them.

items.title: Making a Five-Card Hand
items.content: A player makes the best five-card hand out of the seven cards available: two hole cards and five board cards. A hand always holds exactly five cards.

items.title: Playing the Board
items.content: A player may use two hole cards, one hole card, or no hole card. A player whose best five cards are the five board cards plays the board. Every player who reaches the showdown holds at least the strength of the board.
items.example: The board shows five cards of one suit that run from ten to the ace. Nobody can beat that, so every remaining player plays the board and the pot divides.

items.title: The Burn Card
items.content: Before the dealer puts out the flop, the turn, or the river, the dealer takes the top card of the pack and puts it face down to one side. That card is the burn card. It takes no part in the hand, and no player sees it.

items.title: The Pot and Table Stakes
items.content: The pot holds every chip the players bet during the hand. A player bets only the chips that sat on the table when the hand started. A player adds chips between hands and never during one, and a player never takes chips off the table while a hand runs.

items.title: The Rake
items.content: In a game played for cash, the house takes a fee out of the pot. That fee is the rake. The dealer takes the rake before the winner receives the chips. The house sets the amount, and the rules of the game do not fix it.

items.title: The Button
items.content: A round disc called the button marks the seat that counts as the dealer for one hand. After each hand the button moves one seat clockwise. The button decides where the deal starts and where the action starts.

items.title: The Blinds
items.content: Two players put chips in the pot before they see any card. These forced bets are the blinds. They give every hand a pot to compete for, so a player who folds every hand still pays to sit at the table.

items.title: The Small Blind
items.content: The player on the immediate left of the button posts the small blind before the deal.

items.title: The Big Blind
items.content: The next player clockwise posts the big blind. The big blind is normally twice the small blind.
items.example: At stakes of 25 and 50, the small blind is 25 and the big blind is 50.

items.title: The Big Blind Counts as a Bet
items.content: The big blind counts as the first bet of the pre-flop round. A player who wants to stay in the hand must at least match it. The big blind also sets the smallest bet allowed in a no-limit game.

items.title: Blinds With Two Players
items.content: With only two players in the hand, the player on the button posts the small blind and acts first before the flop. The other player posts the big blind and acts first on every later round.

items.title: Position
items.content: Position names the place a player holds in the action order for a betting round. A player who acts late in the round already knows what the earlier players did.

items.title: Under the Gun
items.content: Before the flop, the player on the immediate left of the big blind acts first. Players call that seat under the gun.

items.title: The Button Acts Last
items.content: After the flop the player on the button acts last in every betting round of that hand.

items.title: The Ante
items.content: Some games ask every player to put a small forced bet in the pot before the deal. That bet is the ante. The ante does not count toward the first bet of the round, so a player must still match the big blind to stay in. The house or the tournament structure sets the size of the ante.

items.title: The Big Blind Ante
items.content: Some tournaments ask one player to post the whole ante for the table. The player in the big blind posts it. This keeps the deal quick, because the dealer collects one ante instead of one from every seat.

items.title: Four Betting Rounds
items.content: A hand holds four betting rounds. They run in this order: pre-flop, the flop, the turn, and the river. A hand ends early if every player but one folds.

items.title: Pre-Flop
items.content: The first betting round starts as soon as every player holds two hole cards. No board card is face up yet. Action starts with the player on the immediate left of the big blind and moves clockwise.

items.title: The Big Blind Option
items.content: If no player raises before the action returns to the big blind, that player may check or raise. The big blind holds this choice because the forced bet already matches the largest bet of the round.

items.title: The Flop
items.content: The dealer burns one card and then turns three board cards face up together. Those three cards are the flop. A betting round follows.

items.title: Action After the Flop
items.content: On the flop and on every later round, the first player still in the hand to the left of the button acts first.

items.title: The Turn
items.content: The dealer burns one card and turns a fourth board card face up. That card is the turn, and players also call it fourth street. A betting round follows.

items.title: The River
items.content: The dealer burns one card and turns a fifth board card face up. That card is the river, and players also call it fifth street. The board is now complete, and the betting round that follows is the last one.

items.title: The End of a Betting Round
items.content: A betting round ends when every player still in the hand has put the same amount in the pot for that round, or has folded. A round in which nobody bets ends when the last player checks.

items.title: Winning Before the Showdown
items.content: If every other player folds, the one player left takes the pot at once. That player wins without showing the hole cards, and the hand ends there.

items.title: The Five Actions
items.content: At their turn a player takes exactly one of five actions: check, bet, call, raise, or fold. The amount already bet in the round decides which of the five the player may take.

items.title: Check
items.content: A player who faces no bet in the current round may check. A check passes the action to the next player and keeps the hand alive at no cost. A player who faces a bet may not check.

items.title: Check-Raise
items.content: A player who checks may still call or raise later in the same round if another player bets. A check followed by a raise in the same round is a check-raise, and the rules allow it.
items.example: The first player checks. The next player bets 200. The first player then raises to 600. That is a legal check-raise.

items.title: Bet
items.content: A player who faces no bet may put chips in the pot. In a no-limit game the smallest bet equals the big blind, and the largest bet equals every chip the player holds on the table.

items.title: Call
items.content: A player puts in chips equal to the largest amount bet in the current round and stays in the hand. A player who already has chips in the round adds only the difference.

items.title: Raise
items.content: A player who faces a bet may put in more than the amount needed to call. A raise reopens the round, so every other player must call the new amount, raise again, or fold.

items.title: The Minimum Raise
items.content: A raise must increase the current bet by at least the size of the last bet or the last raise in that round. Before the flop, the big blind counts as that last bet.
items.example: A player bets 100. The next raise must reach at least 200, because the raise adds at least the 100 that came before it.

items.title: A Short All-In Raise
items.content: A player who goes all in for less than a full raise does not reopen the round. A player who already acted in that round may then call the extra amount or fold, but may not raise again.
items.example: The bet is 100 and a raise must reach 200. A player goes all in for 160. A player who already called the 100 may pay the extra 60 or fold, and may not raise.

items.title: Fold
items.content: A player gives up the hand and every claim to the pot. The player slides the two hole cards face down toward the dealer. Chips the player already put in the pot stay in the pot.

items.title: String Bets
items.content: A player puts the chips in the pot in one motion, or states the whole amount before touching any chip. A player who reaches back for more chips without a spoken amount makes a string bet. The dealer then counts only the chips of the first motion.
items.example: A player pushes 200 forward, sees the next player react, and reaches back for 300 more. The dealer rules the bet at 200.

items.title: A Spoken Action Binds
items.content: A clear statement made at a player's own turn binds that player. A player who says a raise to 500 must put 500 in the pot, even when the chips go in afterwards.

items.title: Acting Out of Turn
items.content: A player acts only at their own turn. An action taken early does not bind the player if the action in front of that player changes. If nothing changes, the dealer holds the player to the early action.
items.example: A player folds out of turn. An earlier player then raises. The fold still stands, because a raise does not help a player who wanted to fold.

items.title: One Oversized Chip
items.content: A player who faces a bet and puts in one chip worth more than the call, with no spoken raise, has called. The dealer returns the difference.
items.example: The bet is 300. A player puts in one chip worth 1000 and says nothing. That is a call of 300, and the dealer returns 700.

items.title: All-In
items.content: A player who puts every remaining chip in the pot is all in. A player may go all in at any turn, whatever the size of the bet in front of them.

items.title: An All-In Player Stays In
items.content: A player who is all in stays in the hand to the showdown. A shortage of chips never pushes a player out of a hand that player already paid for.

items.title: What an All-In Player Wins
items.content: A player who is all in wins only the chips that player matched. Every chip bet above that amount goes to a side pot, and the all-in player cannot win that side pot.

items.title: The Main Pot
items.content: The main pot holds the chips every player still in the hand matched, counted up to the size of the smallest all-in wager. Every player still in the hand may win the main pot.

items.title: A Side Pot
items.content: The dealer builds a side pot from the chips bet above an all-in amount. Only the players who put chips in that side pot may win it. Those players keep betting into it after the all-in player can bet no more.
items.example: Three players see the flop. One goes all in for 500, and the other two each bet 1200. The main pot holds 1500. A side pot of 1400 holds the extra 700 from each of the two players, and only those two can win it.

items.title: More Than One Side Pot
items.content: A second all-in wager of a different size creates a second side pot. The dealer builds one pot for each all-in level, and keeps the pots apart until the showdown.

items.title: The Award Order
items.content: The dealer awards the last side pot first, then works back through the earlier side pots, and awards the main pot last. A player who wins a side pot need not win the main pot as well.

items.title: Cards Face Up When Betting Ends
items.content: When no player still in the hand can bet again, and two or more players remain, those players turn their hole cards face up. The dealer then puts out the rest of the board with no further betting.

items.title: When a Showdown Happens
items.content: A showdown happens after the last betting round when two or more players are still in the hand. The players turn their hole cards face up and compare hands.

items.title: The Show Order
items.content: The player who made the last bet or the last raise on the river shows the hole cards first. If no player bet on the river, the first player still in the hand to the left of the button shows first. The other players then show in clockwise order.

items.title: The Best Hand Wins
items.content: The best five-card hand takes the pot. Suits carry equal weight, so a suit never breaks a tie between two hands.

items.title: A Split Pot
items.content: Two or more hands of equal strength share the pot in equal parts. Only five cards count, so a sixth card never breaks the tie. If the pot does not divide evenly, the extra chip goes to the first of the tied players clockwise from the button.
items.example: The board holds a straight that both players use. Neither player improves it with a hole card, so the two hands match and the pot divides.

items.title: Cards Speak
items.content: The dealer reads every hand that reaches the showdown. The cards decide the winner. A player who names the hand wrongly still wins when the cards on the table hold the best hand.

items.title: The Muck
items.content: The muck is the pile of discarded cards beside the dealer. A player who does not want to show may pass the hole cards face down to the dealer. A hand that reaches the muck is dead and can win nothing.

items.title: A Winner Shows Both Cards
items.content: A player who claims the pot at a showdown turns both hole cards face up. A hand with one card still face down wins nothing.

items.title: The Kicker
items.content: When two players hold the same rank of hand, the highest card outside that rank decides the pot. That card is the kicker. Compare the kickers one at a time, highest first, until one player holds the higher card or until all five cards match.
items.example: Both players pair their kings. One holds an ace beside the pair, the other holds a queen. The ace is the higher kicker, so that player takes the pot.

items.title: The Ranking Order
items.content: Ten ranks of hand exist. From the strongest down to the weakest they are: royal flush, straight flush, four of a kind, full house, flush, straight, three of a kind, two pair, one pair, and high card. A hand of a higher rank beats every hand of a lower rank.

items.title: Royal Flush
items.content: Five cards of one suit that run from ten up to the ace. This is the strongest hand in the game. Two royal flushes can only tie, and the pot then divides.

items.title: Straight Flush
items.content: Five cards of one suit in an unbroken sequence. The highest card of the sequence decides which of two straight flushes wins.

items.title: Four of a Kind
items.content: Four cards of one rank, plus one more card. The rank of the four cards decides which of two such hands wins. If both players use the same four board cards, the fifth card decides.

items.title: Full House
items.content: Three cards of one rank plus two cards of a second rank. The rank of the three cards decides the winner first. If those match, the rank of the pair decides.

items.title: Flush
items.content: Five cards of one suit that do not form a sequence. Compare the highest card first, then the next highest, and so on down the five cards. A suit never decides between two flushes.

items.title: Straight
items.content: Five cards in an unbroken sequence that do not all share one suit. The highest card of the sequence decides which of two straights wins.

items.title: The Ace at Both Ends
items.content: The ace runs high in the sequence ten, jack, queen, king, ace, and low in the sequence five, four, three, two, ace. A sequence never wraps past the ace, so king, ace, two, three, four is not a straight.

items.title: Three of a Kind
items.content: Three cards of one rank plus two unmatched cards. The rank of the three cards decides the winner. If those match, the two remaining cards act as kickers.

items.title: Two Pair
items.content: Two cards of one rank, two cards of a second rank, and one more card. Compare the higher pair first, then the lower pair, then the last card.

items.title: One Pair
items.content: Two cards of one rank plus three unmatched cards. Compare the rank of the pair first. If the pairs match, compare the three remaining cards in order, highest first.

items.title: High Card
items.content: Five cards that match none of the ranks above. The highest card decides, then the next highest, and so on through all five cards.

items.title: The Best Possible Hand
items.content: For any board, one hand is the strongest hand a player can hold. Players call that hand the nuts. The board decides what the nuts is, and each new board card can change it.

items.title: A Dead Hand
items.content: A dead hand can win nothing. A hand dies when the player folds it, when it reaches the muck, when the player exposes it to another player during the hand, or when it holds the wrong number of cards.

items.title: The Wrong Number of Cards
items.content: A hand with more than two hole cards or fewer than two hole cards is dead as soon as the first betting round starts.

items.title: A Misdeal
items.content: The dealer calls a misdeal when the deal goes wrong before real betting action starts. The dealer then takes the cards back, shuffles the whole pack, and deals again with the button in the same seat.

items.title: After Real Action
items.content: Once two players act, or one player bets and one player calls, the hand stands. The dealer corrects what remains and plays the hand out.

items.title: An Exposed Hole Card
items.content: If the dealer turns one hole card face up during the deal, the dealer finishes the deal, gives that player the next card off the pack, and uses the exposed card as the burn card for the flop. If the dealer exposes two cards to one player, the dealer calls a misdeal.

items.title: A Flop With Too Many Cards
items.content: If the dealer turns more than three cards for the flop, the dealer takes those cards back, mixes them into the pack, shuffles, and puts out a new flop.

items.title: One Player To A Hand
items.content: A player plays the hand alone. A player takes no advice about a live hand from anybody, at the table or away from it, and shows the hole cards to nobody while the hand runs.

items.title: The Floor Decides
items.content: A supervisor settles any dispute the players cannot settle. The supervisor puts a fair game and the best interest of the whole table first, and the ruling stands for that hand.

items.title: One Buy-In
items.content: Every player starts a tournament with the same number of chips for the same price. Tournament chips carry no cash value, and a player never takes them off the table. A player who loses every chip leaves the tournament, and the order players leave decides the prizes.

items.title: Rising Blinds
items.content: The blinds rise at set times. Each new level raises the cost of a hand, so the stack a player holds buys fewer hands as the tournament runs on.

items.title: When a Level Changes
items.content: A new level starts with the next hand. A hand already in play finishes under the old level.

items.title: A Short Blind Post
items.content: A player who holds fewer chips than the blind puts every chip in and is all in for that amount. The player stays in the hand and plays for the part of the pot those chips match.
